question: How does fire spread on fabric in microgravity?
answer:
When a thin fuel is ignited in the middle at low forced-flow velocities in microgravity, the flame spreads upstream into the oncoming airflow [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Materials can also burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Flammability is influenced by how the flow field affects the overlap of thermal and species fields in the flame zone [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science].

In microgravity experiments using Nomex fabric, Ultem, and a 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass blend, airflow was directed along the surface in opposed or concurrent directions at speeds reaching up to 40 cm/s [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. Tested fabric sample sizes included 1 to 2 cm [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80].

Our sources do not cover specific numerical flame spread rates for fabrics in microgravity [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80].

question: Which experiments tested oxygen levels above 30%?
answer:
Based on NASA PSI records, four experiments tested oxygen levels above 30% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

- PSI-159 ACME CFI-G tested oxygen concentrations from 12% to 85% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64].
- PSI-10 ACME/Flame Design tested oxygen concentrations from 19.8048% to 84.9978% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-10 · doi:10.60555/w4zy-bt45].
- PSI-20 ACME BRE tested oxygen concentrations from 21% to 40% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-20 · doi:10.60555/vb93-3y72].
- PSI-69 FLEX tested oxygen concentrations from 12% to 34% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

question: How was smoke detection tested on the ISS, and why does it matter?
answer:
On the ISS, smoke detection was examined through experiments including the Dust Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT) for background particulate levels and the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) for smoke particle-size distributions [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. SAME was conducted on the ISS using Comparative Soot Diagnostic Hardware, solid fuels like Teflon and Kapton, 8 experimental test rows, an airflow of 5–10 cm/s, and tools such as smoke detectors, thermophoretic soot samplers, TEM, and video cameras [PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. 

This testing matters because microgravity lacks strong buoyancy-induced flows, leading to larger smoke particles that can alter detector responses compared to terrestrial conditions [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. The quantitative data provides a reduced-gravity baseline to evaluate existing sensors and design advanced fire detectors for long-duration space missions [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-47 · doi:10.60555/ztgj-d202]. Additionally, these developments help improve fire detection technology for extreme Earth environments like submarines and underwater laboratories [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-47 · doi:10.60555/ztgj-d202].

question: What gases were used to put out flames, and in which experiment?
answer:
Nitrogen gas was applied to put out flames in a drop tower test burning a PMMA sphere [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Nitrogen, carbon dioxide, helium, and xenon were used as inert gas suppressants in flammability limit research, with carbon dioxide used in a flame test during the FLEX experiment [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. The FLEX investigation also plans to measure the effectiveness of carbon dioxide, helium, and sulfur hexafluoride as gaseous suppressants [PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451]. 

The sources do not specify which exact gas was used in the BASS experiment, mentioning only a planned objective to test an inert gaseous agent [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80].

question: What happened in the Mir fire in 1997, and what was learned?
answer:
On February 24, 1997, a fire ignited in a solid fuel oxygen generator inside the Kvant-1 module of the Russian space station Mir [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The searing flame lasted several minutes, blocked access to one of two Soyuz escape vehicles, and filled the station's modules with toxic smoke [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The six crew members successfully extinguished the fire with no damage to the station's structure [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Mir's life support systems cleared the atmosphere over several hours, causing no lasting harm to the crew [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir].

Lessons learned were passed on to the design and operations of the International Space Station [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Russian space officials updated emergency crew training, ground controller responses, and ground preparation for oxygen generator canisters [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Consequently, space agencies implemented a robust oxygen generation system with dissimilar redundancies on the International Space Station, alongside additional safety measures for backup oxygen canisters [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir].

question: Is there any fire data for Moon or Mars gravity?
answer:
The NASA PSI Data Repository contains no real partial-gravity combustion data from actual Moon or Mars gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. Within the PSI investigations, one experiment used an electric field to mimic partial gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. 

For lunar gravity, burning cotton-fiberglass blend fabric in air has been observed in simulated lunar gravity using a terrestrial drop tower centrifuge [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. Additionally, the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) investigation is planned as a future experiment to burn materials on the lunar surface [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. 

Our sources do not cover any fire data for Mars gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion].

question: What are cool flames and why are they a risk?
answer:
Cool flames are a low-temperature combustion regime marked by very weak flames that form as an intermediate step between unreacted fuel and oxidizer [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures between 500 and 1000 K [PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64]. They can persist after a visible hot flame extinguishes and burn for a prolonged period while consuming only a fraction of the vaporized fuel [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

Cool flames impact spacecraft fire safety concerns because reduced-gravity environments are particularly conducive to low-temperature combustion [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Understanding cool flames in microgravity helps refine combustion knowledge to support the design of safer spacecraft systems [PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914]. 

Our sources do not cover specific direct hazards, toxic risks, or detailed damage mechanisms of cool flames beyond general spacecraft fire safety concerns [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914].
